whatContradictedTheCard: Two things surfaced that the dispatch did not anticipate, neither in the join design itself. First, a real performance defect: landing_parcel_jurisdiction has no supporting index on place_fips, so the originally-written keyset-paginated per-city query re-scanned the county-restricted range and filtered out ~790,000 non-matching rows on every single page (confirmed live via EXPLAIN ANALYZE, 542ms/page for a 500-row page of a 16,496-row city) -- for a city the size of Austin (218,444 parcels, 437 pages at that rate) this would have been prohibitive. Fixed by switching to a single unpaginated per-city fetch (one scan pays the filter cost once, not once per page) with client-side chunking for the expensive spatial-match phase; re-verified live against Hutto with identical correctness (total/matched unchanged) and materially better wall-clock. Second, a genuine cross-session deploy race: mid-deploy, a concurrent Cloud Build from a peer session was pushing to the same mutable image tag at the same time, and the first deploy attempt pinned to a digest that could not be attributed with confidence to either build. Resolved by waiting for the concurrent build to finish, re-syncing to the then-current origin/main (which had moved again in the interim), and submitting a clean rebuild whose push digest and deploy-pin digest were verified to match exactly before any execution ran. Neither issue was a defect in the spatial-join design itself; both were caught by reading live query plans and live digests rather than trusting either a completed status or a tag name.

The stamp-gap cities' own layer already exists in tx_zoning_district_staging (Smithville 91 features, Luling 140, Martindale 17, Woodcreek 3165, Lakeway 749 per the zoning-ingest close) -- a follow-up card could very plausibly run this exact job against just those five with a small scope change (removing them from STAMP_GAP_EXCLUDED_CITY_KEYS) once the operator explicitly authorizes expanding scope past the stamp-gap boundary this card respected.

A shared-mutable-image-tag race across concurrent Cloud Build submissions from different sessions is a real, now twice-observed hazard on this shared cloudbuild.parcel-record-fill.yaml (once as a code collision on R2, once as a pure deploy-tag race here). No code fix is proposed here since the file is intentionally shared across many small jobs; flagging for the operator in case a per-session build-tag convention is worth adopting.

LESSON: Before trusting a paginated query pattern copied from a similar-looking job, check whether the filter column actually has a supporting index -- landing_parcel_jurisdiction's PK is (county_fips, prop_id) only, so a place_fips-filtered keyset page silently re-scans and discards a huge fraction of the county range on every single page. EXPLAIN ANALYZE caught this in under a minute; the symptom (a small city's job taking 100+ seconds) would have been easy to write off as 'PostGIS is just slow' without it.

A single unpaginated fetch that returns everything into memory is not always the naive/wrong choice -- when the filtered result set is bounded (here, at most ~220K short id strings for the largest city) and the alternative is a repeated unindexed scan, fetching once and chunking client-side for the expensive downstream work is strictly better.

Verify a Cloud Build's deploy by reading that build's OWN log line for the digest it pinned, never by re-querying the artifact registry tag afterward -- the tag is mutable and a concurrent build can race it. This is the same discipline as verifying a Cloud Run digest against the build that produced it, one level earlier in the pipeline.

A sharp per-city outlier in a coverage figure is worth one targeted live query before writing it into a close as an unexplained number. Elgin's 68.7% looked like it could have been a join bug; a single GROUP BY county_fips query showed it was a clean 100%/0% split matching a population size exactly, which is a completely different (and much more defensible) finding than 'roughly two-thirds matched for unclear reasons'.
